In summary, our research is concerned with
the design, development, implementation and analysis of browsing interfaces to digital video information.
developing and evaluating interfaces for digital video which are based on keyframes and which are suitable for browsing.
the design of interfaces which allow a viewer to quickly and easily find and view a particular scene in a video sequence.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the interfaces which provide a combination of temporal information with spatial visualisation are most useful.
there is no "best" browsing interface, but that the choice of interface is dependent on the application domain.
the best browsing interfaces for digital TV programmes have yet to be designed.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
there is no "one size fits all" interface for video browsing.

the most effective browsing interfaces are those that allow users to navigate through a video programme in an intuitive manner and that provide them with the information that they need to make a selection.

we have implemented six interfaces to a digital video browsing system, and have found that users are more likely to use interfaces which are more "layered" (i.e. provide more levels of abstraction) and which are more visually appealing.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is no "one size fits all" solution for a browsing interface for video information and that the best browsing interface will vary depending on the task at hand.
there are many different ways to visualise the video content and that the choice of visualisation depends on the task the user is trying to accomplish.
we believe that a variety of interfaces is needed in order to support a variety of users with a variety of needs.
